data.content: Hi, I'm at the taxi stand outside Bugis Junction near the fountain.
OK, I see you. Pulling up now, white Elantra.
Thanks for the ride! Just noticed the fare is $16.50 — I thought it was $12?

Platform surge record: multipliers, activation time, rider notification.

explanations.rider: Outcome: you are eligible for a refund of the surge differential, S$4.50, to your original payment method (Section 3.3). This decision was made automatically. The surge multiplier was 1.0x at quote time and 1.5x at the start of the trip (E-SRG-01); the quote of S$12.00 was binding at the multiplier in effect when it was given (Section 3.1) and the final fare is S$16.50. The platform's surge record shows that the rider was not notified in the app before the trip started (Section 3.2). The difference of S$4.50 is entirely the surge: the surgeable subtotal is unchanged and the booking fee is exempt from surge (Sections 3.4 and 3.5). Precedent 7.2 (DISP-2026-0142) ruled the same way on the same key facts, a refund of S$3.20. The disputed amount, S$4.50, is under S$10, so the AI ruling is final (Section 6.1). json.stance: The rider asks for a full refund of the $4.50 surge differential because the surge rose after the quote and the rider was never notified.
json.requested_outcome: full refund of the $4.50 surge differential
json.brief: The upfront quote was $12.00 at 1.0x, and the final fare was $16.50, a difference of $4.50 [E-TRP-01][E-PAY-01]. The platform's own record shows the surge rose from 1.0x at quote time to 1.5x at trip start, activated at 21:04:30 [E-SRG-01]. That record also shows rider_notified is false, with no notification method or timestamp [E-SRG-01]. Section 3.2 requires an in-app notification before or at pickup, and none was sent [Section 3.2]. The fare breakdown shows the surgeable subtotal stayed at $9.00 and the whole $4.50 difference is the surge line, so the increase is solely attributable to surge [E-PAY-01][FC-R14]. Under the matrix, an increase without notice earns a full refund of the surge differential [Section 3.3][Section 3.4]. Precedent 7.2 applied the same result to the same facts [Precedent 7.2]. The rider's chat at the end of the trip shows surprise at the fare, which is consistent with never having been told [E-CHT-03]. The driver may say the rider could have seen the price in the app, but the policy places the duty to notify on the platform, and the record shows it was not met [Section 3.2][E-SRG-01].

arguments.point: Surge increased from 1.0x to 1.5x between quote and trip start.
The rider was not notified of the increase, which breaches the mandatory notification requirement.
The entire $4.50 difference is attributable to surge, with the surgeable subtotal unchanged at $9.00.
Policy and precedent give a full refund of the surge differential when the rider was not notified.

weaknesses.point: The rider's chat shows the rider noticed the fare only after the trip ended and did not cancel at pickup. The other side may argue the rider accepted the ride, but the policy ties the refund to notification, not acceptance.
The ticket is the rider's own statement and carries low credibility, though the platform surge and charge records independently support it.

json.stance: The driver asks that any refund be limited to what Section 3.3 strictly supports and that the driver not be penalized for a platform-side surge and notification failure, conceding that the record favors the rider on the core facts.
json.requested_outcome: no fault on the driver; refund, if any, limited to the $4.50 surge differential and borne by the platform
json.brief: The platform's own records show the surge activated at 21:04:30 and that no notification was sent [E-SRG-01]. Nothing in the file shows the driver set the multiplier or controlled rider notifications. Section 3.2 places the in-app notification on the system, and the notification record shows no method or timestamp [Section 3.2][E-SRG-01]. The trip itself matched the estimate at 13 minutes estimated and 13 minutes actual [E-TRP-01], and the GPS pings show a continuous trip from Bugis Junction to Marina Bay Sands with no detour [E-GPS-01][E-GPS-07]. The fare breakdown shows the surgeable subtotal unchanged at $9.00 and the booking fee exempt, so the only difference is the surge line [E-PAY-01][Section 3.5]. Any remedy under Section 3.3 is capped at the surge differential of $4.50, with no added penalty or finding against the driver [Section 3.3][Section 3.4]. The driver did nothing wrong in the conduct of the trip, and the refund should be treated as a platform-level correction.

arguments.point: The surge change and the missing notification are platform-side events, not driver conduct; the file shows no driver action on either.
The trip was performed as estimated, with matching duration and a continuous route, so no other fare component is in dispute.
Any refund is capped at the surge differential of $4.50 and cannot exceed the surge line.
The rider rode to the destination and raised the fare only after the trip ended, which supports that the driver made no misrepresentation about price.

rebuttals.reply: The increase is established, but the record shows it activated at 21:04:30 as a platform surge window and attributes it to no driver action.
The missing notification is shown only as a platform record, and it does not show any driver failure. Section 3.2 does not make the driver the notifier.
Agreed that the difference is the surge line, but this also confirms the remedy is capped at $4.50 and that distance, time and booking fee are not in dispute.
Section 3.3 and Precedent 7.2 support a refund of the differential only, with no additional award. Neither makes the driver responsible for funding it.

concessions.point: Surge rose from 1.0x at quote time to 1.5x at trip start, and the full $4.50 difference is the surge line.
The platform record shows the rider was not notified, so Section 3.3 gives a full refund of the surge differential.

Section 3.2 places the in-app notification on the system, and the notification record shows no method or timestamp [Section 3.2][E-SRG-01]. The trip itself matched the estimate at 13 minutes estimated and 13 minutes actual [E-TRP-01], and the GPS pings show a continuous trip from Bugis Junction to Marina Bay Sands with no detour [E-GPS-01][E-GPS-07]. The fare breakdown shows the surgeable subtotal unchanged at $9.00 and the booking fee exempt, so the only difference is the surge line [E-PAY-01][Section 3.5]. Any remedy under Section 3.3 is capped at the surge differential of $4.50, with no added penalty or finding against the driver [Section 3.3][Section 3.4]. The driver did nothing wrong in the conduct of the trip, and the refund should be treated as a platform-level correction.

arguments.point: The surge change and the missing notification are platform-side events, not driver conduct; the file shows no driver action on either.
The trip was performed as estimated, with matching duration and a continuous route, so no other fare component is in dispute.
Any refund is capped at the surge differential of $4.50 and cannot exceed the surge line.
The rider rode to the destination and raised the fare only after the trip ended, which supports that the driver made no misrepresentation about price.

rebuttals.reply: The increase is established, but the record shows it activated at 21:04:30 as a platform surge window and attributes it to no driver action.
The missing notification is shown only as a platform record, and it does not show any driver failure. Section 3.2 does not make the driver the notifier.
Agreed that the difference is the surge line, but this also confirms the remedy is capped at $4.50 and that distance, time and booking fee are not in dispute.
Section 3.3 and Precedent 7.2 support a refund of the differential only, with no additional award. Neither makes the driver responsible for funding it.

concessions.point: Surge rose from 1.0x at quote time to 1.5x at trip start, and the full $4.50 difference is the surge line.
The platform record shows the rider was not notified, so Section 3.3 gives a full refund of the surge differential.

result.reasoning: The platform surge record shows the multiplier rose from 1.0x at quote time to 1.5x at trip start, activated at 21:04:30, before the trip began at 21:05:00 [E-SRG-01]. The same record shows the rider was not notified, with no method or timestamp [E-SRG-01]. The rider's chat shows no sign of any notice and expresses surprise at the fare after the trip [E-CHT-01][E-CHT-03]. The fare breakdown shows the surgeable subtotal unchanged at $9.00, the booking fee exempt, and the whole $4.50 difference in the surge line, so the increase is solely due to surge [E-PAY-01][E-TRP-01][Section 3.4][Section 3.5]. Section 3.3 gives a full refund of the surge differential when surge rises and the rider was not notified. Precedent 7.2 is ALIGNED on both key factors (surge increased, rider not notified) and gave a full refund of the differential. The rider advocate's point that the duty to notify was unmet is established by platform records. The driver advocate's points that the driver did not cause the surge and that the refund is capped at $4.50 are accepted, and the platform bears the refund. The ticket is only the rider's statement, but the tier A records carry the decision. The amount is under $10, so the ruling is final under Section 6.1. I agree with the engine.

The whole $4.50 difference between the $12.00 quote and the $16.50 fare comes from the surge [E-PAY-01]. Under Section 3.3, a rider who is not told about a surge increase gets the surge differential back. This decision is final under Section 6.1, and you can ask for a human review if you wish.
result.driver_explanation: The rider is getting a refund of $4.50, and the platform pays it, not you. The surge rose from 1.0x to 1.5x before the trip started, and the platform record shows no notification was sent to the rider [E-SRG-01]. Under Section 3.3 the refund is limited to the surge differential, and the records show nothing wrong in how you drove the trip [E-TRP-01][E-PAY-01]. No finding is made against you. You can ask for a human review if you wish.

json.brief: The upfront quote was $12.00 at 1.0x, and the final fare was $16.50, a difference of $4.50 [E-TRP-01][E-PAY-01]. The platform's own record shows the surge rose from 1.0x at quote time to 1.5x at trip start, activated at 21:04:30 [E-SRG-01]. That record also shows rider_notified is false, with no notification method or timestamp [E-SRG-01]. Section 3.2 requires an in-app notification before or at pickup, and none was sent [Section 3.2]. The fare breakdown shows the surgeable subtotal stayed at $9.00 and the whole $4.50 difference is the surge line, so the increase is solely attributable to surge [E-PAY-01][FC-R14]. Under the matrix, an increase without notice earns a full refund of the surge differential [Section 3.3][Section 3.4]. Precedent 7.2 applied the same result to the same facts [Precedent 7.2]. The rider's chat at the end of the trip shows surprise at the fare, which is consistent with never having been told [E-CHT-03]. The driver may say the rider could have seen the price in the app, but the policy places the duty to notify on the platform, and the record shows it was not met [Section 3.2][E-SRG-01].

arguments.point: Surge increased from 1.0x to 1.5x between quote and trip start.
The rider was not notified of the increase, which breaches the mandatory notification requirement.
The entire $4.50 difference is attributable to surge, with the surgeable subtotal unchanged at $9.00.
Policy and precedent give a full refund of the surge differential when the rider was not notified.

weaknesses.point: The rider's chat shows the rider noticed the fare only after the trip ended and did not cancel at pickup. The other side may argue the rider accepted the ride, but the policy ties the refund to notification, not acceptance.
The ticket is the rider's own statement and carries low credibility, though the platform surge and charge records independently support it.
